query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, high-ductility metallic coating (e.g. copper) onto the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will improve its crack‐resistance and overall mechanical integrity while preserving its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples synthesized by standard melting routes that exhibit significant cracking under applied-field/pressure-field operation.
generation.intervention: Deposit a conformal, sub-micron to few-micron thick copper coating via physical vapor deposition (PVD) onto the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Testing under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields and temperature regimes as used in the caloric response measurements (e.g. near room temperature with moderate field cycling) as well as standard compressive loading (e.g., quasi-static strain rate) for mechanical integrity evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, well-adhered metallic film that bridges surface flaws and acts as a crack‐arrest layer at the alloy–coating interface.
generation.mechanism: The copper coating, being ductile and having high toughness, will blunt crack tips and redistribute local stresses during field-induced deformation, thereby raising the effective compressive strength and preventing catastrophic fracture. Because the coating is thin and conformal, it minimally dilutes or perturbs the intrinsic caloric phase transformation mechanisms in the underlying high-entropy matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the compressive strength and improved damage tolerance (i.e., reduced crack propagation) relative to uncoated samples, while the caloric response (magnitude of field- or pressure-induced thermal change) remains essentially unchanged compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The uncoated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows high caloric response but poor mechanical integrity that leads to cracking under operational conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under the same applied-field/pressure conditions and temperature ranges used originally for caloric performance measurements (typically near ambient to moderately elevated temperatures) and under quasi-static compressive loading.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain exactly how the coating thickness and adhesion quality will affect the caloric response; overly thick or poorly bonded coatings might dampen the functional effect or introduce thermal barriers. Optimization of the coating parameters will be necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set receives the optimized PVD copper coating and the other remains uncoated. Subject both sets to identical cyclic applied-field and pressure-field tests while monitoring caloric response, and perform compressive mechanical tests (e.g. quasi-static compression) to assess cracking and yield strength.
measurements: Quantitative caloric effect (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change) under identical field/pressure cycles
Compressive yield strength and plastic strain measurements
Fractography (microscopy) to evaluate crack initiation and propagation
Thermal conductivity at operational temperatures to check for possible interference
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength or crack resistance compared to the uncoated samples, or if the caloric response is measurably reduced (beyond experimental uncertainty) relative to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloy nanopowders were successfully prepared by liquid-phase reduction methods and their applications were preliminarily discussed. The prepared high entropy alloy nanopowders consisted of FeNi alloy spherical powders and NiFeCoCrY alloy spherical powders with a particle size of about 100 nm. The powders have soft magnetic properties, the saturation magnetization field strength were up to 5000 Qe and the saturation magnetization strength Ms was about 17.3 emu/g. The powders have the excellent property of low high-frequency loss in the frequency range of 0.3–8.5 GHz. When the thickness of the powders coating was 5 mm, the powders showed excellent absorption performance in the Ku band; and when the thickness of the powders coating was 10 mm; the powders showed good wave-absorbing performance in the X band. The powders have good moulding, and the powders have large specific surface area, so that the magnetic powder core composites could be prepared under low pressure and without coating insulators, and the magnetic powder cores showed excellent frequency-constant magnetization and magnetic field-constant magnetization characteristics. The microstructure, Vickers hardness, and compressive properties of novel low-activation VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) were studied. The alloys were fabricated by vacuum-arc melting and the characteristics of these alloys were explored. The microstructures of all the alloys exhibited a typical morphology of dendritic and eutectic structures. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys are essentially single phase, consisting of a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase, whereas the VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloy contains fine, nanoscale precipitates distributed in the BCC matrix. The lattice parameters and compositions of the identified phases were investigated. The alloys have Vickers hardness values ranging from 546 HV0.2 to 1135 HV0.2 with the x ranging from 0.1 to 1, respectively. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1341 MPa and 1742 MPa, with compressive plastic strains of 42.2% and 35.7%, respectively. VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys have excellent hardness after annealing for 25 h at 600–1000 °C, and presented compressive yield strength exceeding 1000 MPa with excellent heat-softening
